walkthroughs.body_html:
Geographic Perspectives: Global Change — a core area of Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Geographic Perspectives: Global Change brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Geographic Perspectives: Global Change.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Does the Anthropocene refer only to climate change?
options: No - it describes pervasive human influence across many Earth systems, including land use, biodiversity loss, nutrient cycles and climate.
Anthropocene is just another word for global warming.
The Anthropocene is the geological era when dinosaurs lived.
Planetary boundaries are physical fences built around ecosystems.

mcqs.q: Has globalisation made every place equally connected?
options: No - connectivity is highly uneven; some hyper-connected world cities act as hubs while many regions remain weakly integrated or 'switched off'.
The Anthropocene is the geological era when dinosaurs lived.
Globalisation only involves the movement of physical goods.
Globalisation affects all places to the same degree and makes them similar.

mcqs.q: If a planetary boundary is crossed, does Earth collapse immediately?
options: No - crossing a boundary raises the risk of large-scale, potentially irreversible change; it marks entry into a danger zone, not instant catastrophe.
Globalisation only involves the movement of physical goods.
Crossing any planetary boundary causes immediate global collapse.
Planetary boundaries are physical fences built around ecosystems.
